q: What is the purpose of exploratory data analysis before building a model?
options: To profile, summarise and plot the data to understand its quality
To tune the final model settings until test accuracy stops improving
To deploy a trained model and monitor how it behaves on live data
To replace validation by checking the model against the training set
explain: EDA happens before formal modelling. It builds a picture of the data's content, quality, relationships and anomalies. Tuning, deployment and validation come later.

q: Which of the following can EDA reveal about a dataset?
options: Class imbalance and skewed distributions
Missing values, duplicates and wrong data types
The final accuracy the model will reach on unseen data
Which neural network design will always perform best
Target leakage and sampling bias
explain: EDA finds problems with the data and hints at suitable methods. It cannot give final performance because no model has been tested yet.

q: In the scientific method for AI research, what comes straight after proposing an algorithmic approach as a hypothesis?
options: Conclusion where findings are refined and published
Experimentation using controlled tests on datasets
Observation of a real world problem such as air quality
Analysis of results using quantitative metrics
explain: The order is observation, hypothesis, experimentation, analysis and conclusion. Analysis needs results from the experiment first.

q: Which of the following are reasons AI is valuable in research?
options: It can bridge fields such as biology, health and transport
It can uncover hidden patterns in large and complex datasets
It can automate repetitive cleaning, annotation and analysis
It guarantees correct conclusions without any experiments
It removes the need for reproducibility and peer review
explain: AI accelerates discovery and automates routine work. Research using AI still follows the scientific method with peer review and reproducibility.

q: A researcher checks a model using cross-validation, statistical tests and benchmark comparison. Which stage of the AI research pipeline is this?
options: Problem formulation
Model development
Evaluation and validation
Data collection and preprocessing
explain: Cross-validation, statistical testing and benchmarking check whether the model really works. Choosing and justifying an algorithm belongs to model development.

q: Hourly air quality readings are collected from one sensor over several months and the order of the readings matters. Which data modality fits best?
options: Tabular data
Text data
Image data
Time series data
explain: Time series are observations indexed by time, so order and the dependence between readings matter. Tabular rows are treated as separate entities.

q: Which pair of properties is profiled when exploring audio data?
options: Sampling rate and duration
Tokenisation and vocabulary size
Autocorrelation and seasonality
Shape, aspect ratio and colour channels
explain: Audio is profiled by sampling rate, duration and spectrograms. Tokenisation belongs to text, autocorrelation and seasonality to time series, and shape and channels to images.

q: After joining two tables, many rows appear twice. What does this most likely point to?
options: A genuine extreme value that needs modelling separately
A join that has gone wrong and created duplicates
Seasonality in the underlying process
Class imbalance in the target column
explain: Schema and integrity checks look for duplicated rows and identifier collisions, which signal broken joins. Outliers and imbalance are different problems.

q: One record shows a customer age of 250, while another shows a rare but real very high income. How should each be treated?
options: Both are errors and should be deleted straight away
Both are true extremes and should be left untouched
The age is probably an entry error and the income a true extreme
The income is probably an entry error and the age is a true extreme
explain: A value of 250 cannot be a real age, so it is probably an entry error. A very high income can be real, so it calls for a modelling choice such as a transform, not automatic removal.

q: Why does EDA compare the scales and ranges of features?
options: To remove duplicated rows before the dataset is split
To measure how many values are missing in each column
To choose how the data is divided into training groups
To decide whether features need scaling before modelling
explain: Features with very different ranges can distort distance-based methods and make optimisation unstable. Standard, robust or power scaling may then be used.

q: A feature correlates almost perfectly with the target. What should you suspect first?
options: Target leakage, where the feature reveals the label
A perfect predictor that should simply be kept in the model
Class imbalance in the target column
A skewed feature that needs a log transform
explain: Correlations that are too perfect are a warning of leakage. A model using the leaked feature would look good in testing but fail on real new data.

q: What does multicollinearity describe?
options: How strongly each feature is related to the target label in the data
How strongly each feature can be explained by the other features
How many values in each feature are missing
How evenly the classes are spread across the dataset
explain: Multicollinearity describes how strongly a feature can be explained by the other features. The variance inflation factor measures it and helps decide which variables to drop, combine or regularise. How strongly a feature relates to the target is a different check.

q: A dataset has a rare positive class. Which responses are sensible?
options: Report overall accuracy only because it is the simplest measure
Use stratified splits so each split keeps the class mix
Use class weights or resampling
Judge the model with measures such as F1 or PR-AUC
Delete the rare class so the classes are balanced
explain: Imbalance makes accuracy misleading and can hide poor performance on the rare class. Deleting that class removes the very cases you care about.

q: A dataset holds daily sales for three years and the aim is to forecast the future. Which split design suits it?
options: A random split that shuffles all days together
A stratified split that balances classes
A time-based split where training data comes before test data
A split that places some days from every year in all three sets
explain: The split should reflect how the data were generated. Random shuffling would let the model train on days after the ones it is tested on, which gives overly optimistic results.

q: A dataset has many records for each patient. What split avoids an overly optimistic result?
options: A random split that sends the records of one patient to every one of the sets
A time split that ignores which patient each record belongs to
A stratified split that balances the classes in each set
A grouped split that keeps all records of a patient in the same set
explain: If records of the same patient appear in training and test sets, the model can recognise the person. Grouped entities need grouped splitting.

q: Which of these can a dimensionality check with PCA on standardised data show?
options: Which single feature caused the class label
Two or three dimensional views for sanity checks
The exact number of missing values in each row
Potential for compressing the data
Axes that are noisy or carry little signal
explain: PCA shows how variance is concentrated across directions. It does not prove causes and it is not a missingness check.

q: Which are key properties of time series data?
options: Possible non-stationarity
Trends
Temporal dependence, also called autocorrelation
Seasonality
Rows are independent so order never matters
explain: Order is the defining feature of a time series. Because of this, observations are rarely independent.

q: A series rises steadily so its average changes over time. What is a suitable remedy before modelling?
options: Differencing or detrending to make the series more stable
Scaling every value to the same range
Shuffling the observations so the order of the series is broken
Splitting the series with stratified sampling
explain: A changing mean means the series is not stationary. Differencing and detrending are the standard remedies, and a log transform helps when the variance changes.

q: What does analysing change points help you separate?
options: Seasonal cycles from random sampling error
Brief spikes from lasting shifts in level
Training rows from validation rows
Duplicated timestamps from missing timestamps
explain: A transient spike may be noise while a persistent level change means the data regime shifted. The two need different modelling responses.

q: Why might stop words be removed in a bag-of-words model?
options: They are rare words that make the vocabulary too small
They are the words that carry most of the meaning
They are very common and rarely add task-specific meaning
They are numbers and symbols that cannot be counted
explain: Function words such as the and and dominate counts without telling much about the task. Removing them cuts noise and dimensionality.

q: What caution applies when converting all text to lowercase?
options: It always makes the vocabulary larger and sparser
It removes every punctuation mark in the text
It changes the meaning of every word in all cases
Case can carry meaning in some tasks or languages
explain: Lowercasing merges variants such as AI and ai, which reduces sparsity. The risk is losing meaning when capitalisation matters.

q: Which actions belong to careful text cleansing?
options: Masking URLs and mentions
Normalising Unicode and unescaping HTML
Collapsing extra whitespace
Deleting every rare word from the corpus
Rewriting sentences to improve their grammar
explain: Cleansing should standardise text without changing its meaning. Rewriting and deleting words change what the text says.

q: Why look at bigrams and trigrams rather than only single words?
options: They capture phrases such as product names and idioms
They shorten every document so that all lengths match
They remove noise such as URLs and markup tags
They convert words into numbers in a continuous space
explain: Multiword expressions carry meaning that counts of single words lose. Turning words into numbers in a continuous space is what an embedding does.

q: What does projecting documents into a vector space and reducing dimensions help you see?
options: The exact vocabulary size and word frequencies
Clusters, themes and outliers across the documents
The number of empty or malformed documents
The share of URLs and handles in the text
explain: Embedding plots show structure in the corpus, such as clusters and outliers, and give early evidence of how separable the labels are. Vocabulary counts, empty texts and noise indicators come from other EDA steps.

q: Which methods can find exact or near-duplicate images that might leak across splits?
options: Perceptual hashes for near copies
Raising the resolution of every image
Embedding similarity between images
Cryptographic hashes for exact copies
Comparing per-channel means only
explain: Duplicates across training and test sets inflate results because the model has seen the same picture. Hashes and embeddings detect them.

q: Explain what exploratory data analysis is and why it is done before modelling.
model: Exploratory data analysis is the structured process of profiling, summarising and visualising data to understand its content, quality, patterns, relationships and anomalies. It uses simple statistics such as counts, means and correlations together with plots such as histograms and scatter plots. It is done before modelling because it exposes problems like missing values, outliers and leakage early. It also shows distributions and imbalance, and it guides model choice and a realistic baseline.
points: Defined as profiling, summarising and visualising data
Combines simple statistics with plots
Checks data quality such as missing values and outliers
Informs model choice, baselines and bias detection

q: Describe the stages of the AI research pipeline.
model: The pipeline starts with problem formulation, where objectives and research questions are defined. Next comes data collection and preprocessing, which establishes reliability and ethics. Model development follows, with algorithm selection and a justification for the choice. Evaluation and validation then use cross-validation, statistical tests and benchmark comparison. The last stage is knowledge contribution, meaning new methods, insights or applications. The module focus is on the data stages.
points: Problem formulation defines objectives and questions
Data collection and preprocessing covers reliability and ethics
Model development involves choosing and justifying an algorithm
Evaluation uses cross-validation and benchmarks, and knowledge contribution gives new methods or insights

q: Explain how AI research follows the scientific method.
model: AI research starts with observation of a real world problem such as air quality or medical diagnosis. The researcher forms a hypothesis by proposing an algorithmic or modelling approach. Experimentation then tests it with controlled tests on datasets. Results are analysed with quantitative metrics. The conclusion refines the models, generalises the findings and publishes them. As in traditional science, reproducibility and peer review are emphasised.
points: Observation of a real problem
Hypothesis proposes an approach and experimentation tests it
Analysis uses quantitative metrics
Conclusion and publication with reproducibility and peer review

q: Describe how missing values and outliers are investigated in tabular data and what decisions the checks inform.
model: For missing values you measure where data are missing, how much, and whether gaps occur together or relate to the outcome. This shows which columns need imputing or dropping and warns of possible bias. For outliers you use robust rules such as the interquartile range and then inspect the flagged rows. The aim is to separate data entry errors from true extremes. Errors are fixed or removed, while real extremes lead to capping, transforming or choosing a model that copes with them.
points: Missingness is measured by column, proportion and pattern
It informs imputation or dropping and flags bias
Outliers are found with robust rules and then inspected
Errors are separated from legitimate extremes before deciding what to do

q: Explain why the way data is split into training, validation and test sets must reflect how the data were generated. Give one example.
model: The test set should give an honest estimate of how the model performs on new data. If the split ignores how the data arose, information leaks and results look better than they really are. For independent rows a random or stratified split is fine. For data over time a time-based split keeps the past in training and the future in testing. When several records belong to the same person or group, they must stay together in one set.
points: Splits must allow honest estimates of generalisation
Wrong splits cause optimistic bias
Random or stratified for independent rows
A correct example such as time-based or grouped splits

q: Explain what class imbalance is, why it matters and how EDA helps you respond.
model: Class imbalance means some classes or target regions occur much less often than others. It matters because a model can score high overall accuracy by favouring the common class while missing the rare one. EDA checks the class proportions early. If imbalance is found you can use stratified splits so each set keeps the mix, choose metrics such as F1 or PR-AUC, and apply class weights or resampling.
points: Defines imbalance as unequal class frequencies
Accuracy can hide poor performance on the rare class
Checked by looking at class proportions
Responses include stratified splits, better metrics, weights or resampling

q: Describe the key properties of time series data and explain why stationarity is checked.
model: A time series is a set of observations indexed by time and kept in order. The spacing can be regular or irregular and there may be one variable or several. Key properties are temporal dependence, which is autocorrelation, trends, seasonality and possible non-stationarity. Stationarity means the mean, variance and autocovariance stay stable over time. It is checked because trends or changing variance can break many models, and differencing, detrending or log transforms can remedy this.
points: Observations are ordered in time
Names properties such as autocorrelation, trend and seasonality
Stationarity means stable mean, variance and autocovariance
Remedies such as differencing, detrending or transforms

q: Explain stop-word removal, case normalisation and text cleansing, and give the main caution for case normalisation and for cleansing.
model: Stop word removal drops very common function words such as the and and, which cuts noise and dimensionality in bag of words models. Case normalisation usually lowercases text so variants like AI and ai merge, which reduces sparsity, but case can carry meaning in some tasks. Text cleansing standardises text by normalising Unicode, unescaping HTML, masking URLs and collapsing whitespace. It should be minimally invasive so that informative tokens and meaning are kept.
points: Stop words are frequent words removed to reduce noise
Case normalisation merges variants but may lose meaning
Cleansing standardises text through steps such as masking URLs
Cleaning should preserve meaning

q: Describe the main checks made when exploring image data and explain why duplicates are a problem.
model: An image is an array of pixel values with spatial dimensions and one or more channels. EDA profiles resolution and aspect ratio to set target shapes and padding rules. It also checks channel statistics such as means, ranges and colour space, which guide normalisation and can reveal greyscale stored as colour. Quality checks look for blur, over or under exposure and corrupt files. Duplicates matter because the same or near identical image in both training and test sets leaks information and inflates results.
points: Images are pixel arrays with dimensions and channels
Resolution and aspect ratio profiling
Intensity and channel statistics and quality checks such as blur
Duplicates across splits cause leakage and optimistic results

q: Name the main data modalities and give one thing you would profile for each.
model: Tabular data has rows as entities and columns as features, so you check types, duplicates and missing values. Time series data is ordered, so you look at autocorrelation and seasonality. Text is profiled through tokenisation, vocabulary and length statistics. Images are profiled by shape, aspect ratio and channels. Audio is profiled by sampling rate, duration and spectrograms. Video adds frame rate, resolution and colour depth. Each modality needs its own EDA workflow.
points: Lists at least four modalities correctly
Gives a suitable profiling item for tabular and time series
Gives suitable items for text, image or audio
Notes that each modality needs its own EDA workflow

q: Explain the significance of exploratory data analysis in a machine learning project. Discuss three techniques commonly used in EDA and what each shows. What are the consequences of doing too little EDA before building a model?
model: Exploratory data analysis helps us understand the characteristics, structure and quality of a dataset before building a model. It finds patterns, relationships and problems in the data. Descriptive statistics such as mean, median, standard deviation, minimum and maximum show the distribution and spread of numerical features. Visualisation with histograms and box plots shows distributions, skewness and outliers. Correlation analysis shows relationships between numerical variables and possible multicollinearity. Too little EDA can leave missing values, outliers, wrong data types or highly correlated features undetected. These harm training, give misleading results and lower predictive performance, so EDA guides the choice of preprocessing and algorithm.
points: EDA shows the structure, quality and patterns of the data before modelling
Descriptive statistics show distribution and spread
Histograms or box plots show skewness and outliers
Correlation analysis shows relationships and multicollinearity
Too little EDA leaves missing values, outliers or wrong types that harm the model
flag: The model answer follows the tutor's sample answer in the mock test.

q: Which is the most appropriate method for identifying possible outliers in a continuous numerical variable?
options: Pie chart
Box plot
Bar chart
Confusion matrix
explain: A box plot shows the spread of a numerical variable and marks points beyond the whiskers as possible outliers. Pie and bar charts suit categories, and a confusion matrix evaluates a classifier.
source: Tutor's mock test, multiple choice question 1

q: Which statement about a correlation coefficient of -0.85 is correct?
options: The variables have a strong negative linear relationship
One variable causes the other to decrease
The variables have a weak positive relationship
The relationship must be nonlinear
explain: A value near -1 means a strong negative linear relationship. Correlation does not show cause.
source: Tutor's mock test, multiple choice question 2
